newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - bears see reasons for cheer.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - bears see reasons for cheer.

text.p: Bearish sentiment appeared to be in the offing this week for most U.S. oil product market sectors as warmer weather and rising heating oil supplies looked to be coinciding in the key Northeast market.
"I think people are going to be looking for homes for the barrels in New York Harbor (NYH)," said one trader. "No one has ever seen this amount come in at this time of year."
What's more, the return of two key gasoline-making refinery units look likely to loosen U.S. unleaded markets that have seen tight supplies drive prices up recently.

Still, traders said that the Colonial Pipeline will remain full at least through the end of November due to heating oil supply concerns. Colonial rationed shipments on the Houston-to-New York line about a month ago amid concerns that heating oil stocks were just too low for comfort ahead of winter.
Heating oil stocks on the East Coast, the biggest heat oil market in the world, were just under 30 million barrels as of November 8, about 32 percent below prior year levels.

Traders said although there had been little change in the level of distillate inventories in the past week, the market's nervousness about stock levels appeared to have abated. The industry, led by the American Petroleum Institute, had done a good job of explaining that exports and stocks fed just five percent of consumption, while at the same time pumping up distillate production to record levels, the traders said.

Meanwhile, U.S. Gulf Coast (USG) players appeared to have picked up distillate barrels to make sure they would preserve their space on the Colonial. That could spell a glut at the other end of the line in NYH spot markets, traders said.
The outlook in gasoline was, for the moment, also a touch amibiguous, with remnants of past tightness seen persisting, though not likely through the end of the week.
"From November 20th onwards, the gasoline market will loosen with cargo availability coming on," one player said.
He said NYH gasoline grades should see some strength during the early part of the week, helped by heating oil, which is expected to continue elbowing gasoline barrels out of the Colonial Pipeline.

In addition, European gasoline prices remain very strong, which could create competition for the increased production from South America, according to Paulo Nery, analyst with Pace Consultants in Houston.
"There could be a short-term shortage in gasoline, but not very long lasting," Nery said, echoing talk gasoline cargoes are heading here from Europe, despite the strength there.

Traders were also keeping their eyes open for the increased production from a catalytic cracker at Petroleos de Venezuela SA's Amuay refinery. The cracker, which was out of service since Oct. 20, was expected to be back up at its previous level by the end of last week.
Additionally, Sun Co Inc said it had successfully restarted on Monday morning the 85,000 barrel per day catalytic cracker at its Marcus Hook, Pennsylvania refinery near Philadelphia.

But continuing maintenance at Amerada Hess Corp's cat cracker at its huge refinery on St Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands in the eastern Caribbean is likely to keep a solid floor on prices through mid-December, when the work is done.
Strong gasoline prices in the mid-continent may meanwhile also support NYH gasoline prices early in the week, boosting competition for USG barrels, traders said.
West Coast traders forecast a sideways products market this week, with little support from technicals and downward pressure from ample supplies.
